div.p: Philippus
A single pentameter Hail, Paphian goddess: for your power is everlasting,
your deathless beauty and your honoured awe—
all mortal men, the creatures of a day,
revere you in their every word and every noble deed;
for everywhere, to all alike, you show your honour clear.
Socrates
Polycrates: Blessed Pythagoras, Heliconian scion of the Muses,
tell me, since I ask: how many in the contest of wisdom
are in your halls, contending nobly for the prize?
Pythagoras: I will tell you, then, Polycrates. Half of them
press on toward the fair branches of learning; a fourth
labour over the nature of the immortal; a seventh
are wholly given to silence, and to imperishable inward words;
three are women, and Theano excels the rest.
So many ministers of the Muses I myself lead on.
Anonymous Epigrammatists

On the little poem of John the Grammarian The image-maker dared to paint what no portrait may lawfully show, and eloquence brought to completion a deceptive likeness of the world, near to the truth — yet the painting falsified everything.
Damagetus
I am a wrestler neither from Messene nor from Argos; Sparta, glory of men, is my homeland. Those are men of art; but I, as befits the sons of the Lacedaemonians, prevail by force.
Phaedimus
A trimeter Callistratus, the youth of Cephisia,
set up for you, O messenger of Zeus,
this likeness shared with one of his own age:
delight in it, and keep Apollodorus' son and city safe.
Anonymous epigrammatists
On a statue of Pallas Golden Pallas am I, of beaten gold; and the gold
is the gift of vigorous men, the followers of song.
Half the gold Charisius gave, and an eighth part
Thespis, and a tenth part Solon gave,
a twentieth Themison; and the remaining talents,
nine of them, and the workmanship, are the gift of Aristodicus.
Anonymous Epigrammatists

On the city of Myra in Lycia This wall of the city of fair dancing-grounds was raised on high by the sceptred Marcian, at the prompting of the prefect Palladius, and by the ordinances of prudent Artemeon; and the city in time recovered its former measure.
Simonides

Know, when you behold him, Theognetus the Olympic victor, the boy, the skilful charioteer of the wrestling-ring, fairest to look upon, and in the contest no worse than his form, who crowned the city of his noble fathers.
Theocritus
A limping trimeter Here lies the poet Hipponax.
If you are base, do not draw near the tomb;
but if you are honest, of decent stock,
sit down and take your ease, and sleep if you will.
Anonymous epigrammatists
Cypris addressed Eros as he hung his head:
"What grief, my child, has come upon you?" And he answered:
"The Pierians have plundered my apples, one this way, one that,
snatching them from my lap—those I was bringing from Helicon.
Clio took a fifth part of the apples; a twelfth
Euterpe; bright Thalia got an eighth;
Melpomene carried off a twentieth; Terpsichore
a fourth; and Erato came after for a seventh part;
Polymnia robbed me of thirty apples,
and Urania of a hundred and twenty; and Calliope
has gone off weighed down with three hundred apples.
So I come to you with lighter hands,
bringing these fifty apples, what the goddesses have left."
Anonymous Epigrammatists
On the tomb of Saint Nicander Seventeen years old, a child unstained and undefiled, God made me, Nicander, his faithful martyr.
Simonides
At the Isthmus and at Pytho Diophon, son of Philon, won the long jump, the foot-race, the discus, the javelin, the wrestling.
Anacreon
A tetrameter You, Aristocleides, of all my friends I pity first:
you lost your youth defending your homeland from slavery.
Anonymous epigrammatists
On the dung of Augeas The mighty strength of Alcides asked Augeas,
inquiring after the multitude of his herds; and he answered:
"By the streams of Alpheus, friend, are half of them;
an eighth part graze about the hill of Cronus;
a twelfth, far off, beside the shrine of Taraxippus;
a twentieth feed about divine Elis;
a thirtieth I have left behind in Arcadia;
and the rest of the herds, these fifty, you see here."
Anonymous Epigrammatists

A funeral inscription at Nicaea, near the lake, upon the obelisk Boast, Nicaea, of this tomb that storms the heavens, and of this pyramid, neighbour to the sun; it hides the hierophant, famed among the living, buried within this immeasurable monument. This is the great barrow of Sacerdos, this the memorial of Severa, whose neighbour is heaven, not Hades.
Anonymous Epigrammatists
What words might Hector speak as he is wounded by the Greeks Cast now at my body after my death, since even hares insult the corpse of a dead lion.
Phalaecus
A curtailed or docked trimeter "I win the double course." "But I am a wrestler."
"And I the pentathlon." "But I am a boxer." —
"And who are you?" "Timodemus." "But I am a Cretan."
"And I am Cretheus." "But I am Diocles." —
"And who is your father?" "Cleinus." "As mine is too." — "And where do you win?" "At the Isthmus." "And you?" —
"In the Nemean meadow, and at Hera's shrine."
Anonymous epigrammatists
I am the dark child of a white father, a wingless bird,
flying up even to the clouds of heaven;
and to the maidens who meet me I give birth to tears without grief;
yet, born straightway, I am dissolved into the air.
Anonymous Epigrammatists

Heavenly is the monument and the gold-wrought beam of light of the man who found a tomb the equal of his life, neighbour to the stars; it bears such a man as no tomb ever held, the minister of the heavenly mystery, who lifted up his fallen homeland from the ground, who won the highest honours of mind and of speech; for whom Attica strove, she who set his corpse upon the fire, and she who received his bones into her bosom.
Alcaeus
Xerxes too led the Persian army to the land of Hellas, and Titus led one from broad Italy; but the one came to lay the slave's yoke upon the neck of Europe, the other to free Hellas from slavery.
Phalaecus
The eleven-syllable trimeter, so called This portrait, the surpassing image
of the man who made the world laugh in comedy,
crowned for his triumph with ivy and with garlands,
I have set up, that it may mark Lycon's grave.
For all that he was once a shining man . . .
a memorial of that man of charm, in the gathering-place
and over the wine, this stands for those who come after,
a token left behind, an image of his face.
Anonymous epigrammatists
Best of the keepers of the hours, how much of the day has passed?
As much as twice two-thirds of what is gone is what remains.
Anonymous Epigrammatists

This great monument of great Sacerdos was wrought, all-radiant, an earthly star of Ascania, facing the sunbeams; and within, the spirit lies at peace, he who stretched out his right hand even to his homeland as it lay prostrate, and bound about his brows the holy garland, renewed for the son from the father; his homeland received him, a beloved corpse, Attica hallowed him on the pyre, and all the cities of Hellas revere him.
Anonymous Epigrammatists

The lord of Europe, who both on sea and on dry land was as much a king over mortals as Zeus over the immortals, to Hecate of the wayside dedicated the spoils of bold Ciroadas, and of his children, and of all the Odrysian land, this son of Demetrius of the goodly ash-spear; but the glory of Philip has again gone close to the thrones of the gods.
6a. Panteleus

Panteleus On Callimachus and Cynegirus O empty toil and fruitless war! What shall we say to our king of these immortals? O king, why did you send me against immortal warriors? We strike, they do not fall; we wound, they do not fear. One man alone has plundered a whole army; and in their midst he stands all bloody, the unwearied image of Ares, he stands like a tree upon iron roots, and will not fall; but soon he comes, within the ships. Cast off, helmsman; let us flee the threats of the dead.
Callimachus
A comic tetrameter Menoetas of Lyctus dedicated this bow,
saying as he laid it down: "Here, I give you the horn and the quiver,
Sarapis; the Hesperitae keep the arrows."
Anonymous epigrammatists
I am a lion of bronze; and my fountains are my two eyes,
and my mouth, and the sole of my right foot.
My right eye fills the bowl in two days,
my left in three, and the sole of my foot in four;
six hours suffice to fill the mouth. With all at once,
mouth and eyes and foot together, say in what time.
Anonymous Epigrammatists

My homeland is Nicaea, my father the revealer of heaven's mysteries, and I am the heir of the rite; he it was who rescued my city, when it was shaken, from Hades by the gifts of Italian Zeus; I die far from Ascania, and upon the land of ancient Attica I mounted the pyre. A conspicuous monument was won for me by my son, namesake of his grandfather; and his virtue looks to us both.
Alcaeus

Mixing a harmonious sound with the soft pipes, Dorotheus breathed out the woes of the Dardanians, and the thunder-pang of Semele's labour, and he breathed the deeds of the horse, touching the ever-living Graces; he alone, among the prophets of holy Dionysus, escaped the swift wings of blame, a Theban by birth, son of Sosicles; and in the temple of Lyaeus he set up his mouth-band and his reeds.
Theodoridas
The Hesperitae. An Archilochian tetrameter This hammered cauldron of bronze, won by his speed in the long race,
the son of Aristomachus carried off as his prize.
Anonymous epigrammatists
Six, one, five, two, three, four—so the die runs on.
Anonymous Epigrammatists
Alcaeus

No more upon pine-nurturing Phrygia, as once, will you play, sounding your strain through the well-bored reeds, nor any more in your hands shall the work of Tritonian Athena, as before, blossom forth, nymph-born Satyr. For now your hands are bound in inescapable fetters, because, a mortal, you matched yourself against Phoebus in a divine contest. And the pipes, sounding sweet as the lyre, gave you from the contest not a crown, but death.
Callimachus
A bacchic pentameter. The epigram is not complete. Many an amphora comes cleaving the Aegean from the vineyards of Chios,
and many a one bringing the choice nectar of the Lesbian vine.
Anonymous epigrammatists
My father-in-law killed my husband, and my husband killed my father-in-law,
and my brother-in-law his father-in-law, and my father-in-law his own father.
Flavius Cyrus
An encomium on Theodosius the emperor

You bear all the renowned works of the son of Aeacus, save the love that ambushed him; you shoot your arrows like Teucer, yet you keep no bastard's lot, and you have a glorious form, the form of Agamemnon, but wine does not stir your wits; in prudence I liken you wholly to keen-witted Odysseus, yet far from the wicked guiles; and of the old man of Pylos you distil an equal honey-sweet voice, my king, before in time you reach and touch the third generation.
Anonymous Epigrammatists
O belly, you dog-fly, through whom flatterers and parasites sell the law of freedom for a bowl of broth.
Callimachus
A tetrameter of sixteen syllables. This too is incomplete. O ship, that snatched from me the one sweet light of my life,
I beg you, by Zeus the watcher of the harbour . . .
Anonymous epigrammatists
I have learned that cauldrons are not ones to keep silent,
but rather urge the bronze to ring out true,
the first striking back its echo to the second,
and the third passing it on to the fourth.
But if the mover stays at rest and does not blow,
the cauldron is voiceless; for by nature it is no chatterer.
The nature of your cauldrons, indeed, is fair of mouth;
yet meeting yours it grows fairer still of mouth,
silent when it must be, and speaking when it should.
Anonymous Epigrammatists
Whence found we witnesses upon the deep? Tell us, you rocks, tell us, you long waves, with how many storms they battled. The ship was broken, the mast fell, the keel sank, the cargo was lost.
Simonides
A pentameter for the dance
A. Who set up this statue? B. Dorieus of Thurii.
A. Was he not Rhodian by birth? B. Yes, before he fled his homeland,
having done with terrible hand many deeds of violence.
Anonymous epigrammatists
The thousand staters that I have gained
I bid my two sons take;
but let the legitimate one's fifth be increased
by ten of the fourth measure that falls to the bastard.
Anonymous Epigrammatists

In the citadel of Lindus Wide is the fame of ancient Lindus, who upon her heights that touch the sky received the Unwearied Maiden; but greater still upon the earth grew the lovely renown of the virgin, when she was filled with grey-eyed graces. For now the place cries aloud that it is the flourishing house of Athena, looking out upon the fruit-bearing crags; this sweet offering the priest Aglochartus gave to Athena, sharing it from his own possessions, stronger than the lands of Celeus and of Icarius wholly to increase the holy olive.
Hermocreon

Sit beneath this shady plane-tree, stranger, as you pass by, whose leaves Zephyrus stirs with his gentle breath, where Nicagoras set me up, glorious Hermes son of Maia, guardian of the fruitful field and of its goods.
Hegesippus
A trimeter sung in answer to a hexameter Cursed be that day, and the deadly dark,
and the dread roaring of the wind-tossed sea,
that once overturned the ship on which that man, so sweet of soul,
prayed in vain to the gods for the Abderites;
for it was wrecked through all, and driven by the surge
upon rough Seriphus, where, granted fire
by the hands of reverent hosts, he came at last to his homeland,
Abdera, his ashes wrapped in an urn of bronze.
Anonymous epigrammatists
King Croesus dedicated six bowls of six minae,
each one larger than the next by a drachma.
Leo the Philosopher
Anonymous Epigrammatists
Come, and sit beneath my pine, which, leaning toward the soft west winds, makes its honeyed murmur; behold too the honey-dripping spring, where, piping, I bring sweet sleep with my lonely reeds.
Anonymous epigrammatists
A pentameter upon a hexameter, then a trimeter Pyres, the dear son of Polymnestus, dedicated this,
having vowed a tithe to Pallas Tritogeneia;
Cresilas of Cydonia wrought it.
Anonymous epigrammatists
Together we two weigh twenty minae,
Zethus and his kinsman; but if you take from me
a third, and the fourth part of this Amphion here,
finding the whole to be six, you will find our mother's weight.
Constantine

On his own throne If you are wise, sit down; but if of the Muse with your fingertip you have only barely tasted, . . . stand far from me, and seek your seat elsewhere; for I am a chair that carries men who know wisdom.
Plato
Sit beside this lofty, vocal pine that shivers its cone beneath the thick west winds, and beside my plashing streams the pipe shall bring deep slumber upon your charmed eyelids.
Simonides
A pentameter upon a hexameter and two trimeters, then a hexameter Here lies Dandes of Argos, runner of the stadium,
who brought glory to his horse-pasturing homeland with his victories—
twice at Olympia, three times at Pytho,
twice at the Isthmus, fifteen times at Nemea;
and his other victories it is not easy to count.
Anonymous epigrammatists
One wind; two ships; ten sailors row;
and one helmsman steers them both.
Theophanes the Confessor
A reply to this

And what special mark do you bear, O vainglorious one, that you love the wise and drive away the unlettered? You wear no gold, no silver, no ivory, but the men who are masters of carpentry made you, ignorant of Calliope and untaught of Hephaestus, to be a wooden seat for the wise and the unwise alike.
Zenodotus
Who carved Love and set him beside the fountains, thinking to quench this fire with water?
Anonymous epigrammatists
A pentameter upon two hexameters I am Dicon, son of Callimbrotus; and I won
four times at Nemea, twice at Olympia, five times at Pytho,
three times at the Isthmus; I crown the city of Syracuse.
Anonymous epigrammatists
Six feet, in six places, measure out the iambic line:
spondee, choree, dactyl, and anapaest,
pyrrhic and iamb; and each has its own house.
The pyrrhic's end is one that knows a long at the start;
the first and the third and the fifth hold these.
The others march alike along the whole path;
only the lordly iamb the place receives, wherever it will.
Constantine

On the cross which he dedicated in Lindus Constantine, son of John and Eudocia, made me, his glorious offering, whom proud Lindus brought forth as a man more excellent than the former generation, a faithful servant of the sceptred Leo; with whom his brother Alexander and his son Constantine together led the god-supported sceptres of the empire.
Anonymous Epigrammatists

He who once was ever drunk with the wine-spring of Bromius, the goat-footed Satyr, companion of the revellers, bound in fetters about his double legs, forges arms for the child of the goddess Thetis, plying no skilful work of his craft, but rescuing a poor livelihood from his toils.
15a. Anonymous Epigrammatists

a. Where are those cups of yours, glutton? Where the fair frames of the thyrsus, and the revels, leaping-footed Satyr? Who fastened upon you, near the carving-knives, the foot-binding band, and set you, who once swathed yourself in the swaddling-clothes of Bromius? b. Unseemly want, and all-daring necessity, which set me beside Hephaestus, a drinker of cinders.
Anonymous epigrammatists
A pentameter upon three hexameters. Kings of Sparta were my fathers and my brothers;
and I, Cynisca, victorious with my chariot of swift-footed horses,
set up this statue. I declare that I alone of women
in all Greece have won this crown.
Anonymous epigrammatists
A whole island, the lowing of an ox, and the voice of a money-lender.
Constantine

On the same cross Every work falls short of your worth, O Mistress of the world, beyond all wonder; for your glory is beyond all works and beyond decay; yet this work, which Constantine has offered you, is worthy, if indeed, O Virgin, it well portrays the sceptre of your offspring, and the thrice-blessed Passion of his flesh.
Anonymous Epigrammatists
Everything in excess is unfitting; for there is an old saying, that even of honey the surplus turns to gall.
Anonymous epigrammatists
A dimeter upon a hexameter Iphion painted this with his own hand,
he whom the water of Pirene once nourished.
Anonymous epigrammatists
The hunt is a rehearsal for war; the hunt teaches
to seize the hidden, to await the attacker, to flee, to pursue.
Constantine

On the icon of the Mother of God If anyone wished to paint you, O Virgin, he would need the stars rather than colours, that you might be drawn with lights, as the gate of light; but these things do not yield to the words of mortals; so what nature has granted and the law of painting, with these we depict and portray you on our part.
Anonymous Epigrammatists

O Pan, sound the holy strain for the feeding flocks, sending your curved lip over the golden reeds, that the goats may carry to the house of Clymenus their udders heavy with the gifts of white milk, and that for you the husband of the she-goats, standing fairly at your altars, may belch crimson blood from his shaggy breast.
Parmeniscus
An eleven-syllable line upon a hexameter Works of bronze, proclaim the victory of the swift filly,
who, goaded into a charge, threw off her rider
and, riderless, raced over the level course. From that time on
Parmenon won the golden victory.
Phocritus, to your son the Amyclean kings
granted to win the prizes of his fathers.
Anonymous epigrammatists
Hector—the man Diomedes slew, that other Hector,
Ajax, who fought before the Trojans with his spear.
Anonymous Epigrammatists
Anonymous Epigrammatists
Delight your mind by borrowing; but to the moneylenders leave the finger-bending pain of counting their pebbles.
Simonides
A nine-syllable line upon a hexameter Nicoladas of Corinth, who won the victory
at Delphi in the foot-race, dedicated this offering,
and at the Panathenaea took five crowns in the contests,
amphorae of oil one after another;
at the holy Isthmus three times in a row
the shore of the Lord of the Sea knew him take the prize;
three times he won at Nemea, and four more times
at Pellene, twice in the Lycaean games,
and at Tegea, and at Aegina, and at mighty Epidaurus,
and at Thebes, and among the people of Megara;
and in the stadium at Phlius, winning all five events,
he gladdened the heart of great Corinth.
Anonymous epigrammatists
I once saw a beast running upright on its back
through a wood cut by iron, its feet not touching the ground.
Anonymous Epigrammatists

On a certain physician, Asclepiades The physician Asclepiades carried off a girl by force. And after the ruin of the marriage won by abduction he called a crowd to the lawless wedding, of dancing men and wretched women; but the house collapsed in the evening, and all were brought down to the halls of Hades, corpses lay fallen upon corpses; and the stately bridal chamber, woven of roses, dripped crimson blood from the slaughter.
Anonymous Epigrammatists
"Peace to all," said the bishop as he came in. How can he give to all what he alone holds within?
19a. Herodicus

Flee, you followers of Aristarchus, over the broad back of the sea, flee Hellas, more cowardly than the tawny fawn, corner-buzzers, monosyllable-men, who care for their sphin and sphoin, and the min and the nin. Let this be your portion, you blustering ones; but for Herodicus may Hellas ever remain, and god-born Babylon.
Simonides
Upon a hexameter, alternating, the comic tetrameter short by two syllables and the limping Archilochian trimeter
Glorifying his homeland, the holy city of Athena's people,
Opis, child of the dark earth, fashioned these lovely pipes
together with Hephaestus, and dedicated them to Aphrodite,
mastered by his longing for the lovely Bryson.
Anonymous epigrammatists
If you set in the midst of blazing fire its hundred,
you will find the son and the slayer of a maiden.
Palladas
Palladas
When I saw the orator Maurus, the thick-lipped, I marvelled at him, the white-robed demon of the rhetorical art.
Theodoridas
Upon the regular trimeter a dimeter taken from the dance pentameter This is the tomb of Mnasalces of Plataea,
the maker of elegies;
and his Muse was a torn-off fragment
of Simonides' broad style—
empty in its clamour, a flask-thumping bawler of dithyrambs.
He is dead—let us not throw at him; but if he lived,
he would be banging on his drum.
Anonymous epigrammatists
Casting into the midst of Hephaestus a single hundred,
you will find the son and the slayer of a maiden.
Theocritus

Bedfellow of no one, and mother of Far-fighting War, she bore the swift guide of the midwife counter-rock, not Cerastes, whom once the bull-fathered one reared, but him whose end once burned away the mind before the shield's rim, a whole name, of double nature, who held the longing of the windswept, voice-bearing daughter of Merops; who fashioned a shrill song for the violet-crowned Muse, a wound, an ornament of fire-crackling desire; who quenched the equal-voiced manhood of the grandfather-slain, and the Tyrian . . . , to whom Paris Simichidas set this lovely possession of the blind-bearing one. A soul, O cattle-treading, gadfly of the standing Saettan, of stolen father, fatherless, chest-limbed, rejoicing, may you sing sweetly to the mute girl, to Calliope, unseen.
Anonymous Epigrammatists

On Nicholas, Patriarch of Alexandria He who subdued kings and stilled the violence of his adversaries, for the sake of his fathers' good order, he lies beneath this small monument, having become Nicholas, high priest of Christ. But his virtue, rich in blessings, flew to the ends of the world, and his soul attends the chambers of the blessed. For such a life he longed while he was upon the earth, oppressing his fair body with glorious toils.
Phaedimus
Upon the regular trimeter a heroic tetrameter as refrain, limping at the next-to-last The bow with which you slew the Giant's strength,
restrain its force, far-shooting lord:
. . . his wolf-slaying quiver is not unloosed;
but turn upon these young men an arrow
of Eros, that they may defend their homeland,
made bold by their love of youths;
for it kindles valour, and this, the highest of the gods,
ever exalts the champions in the front.
And you, ancestral glory of the men of Schoenus,
receive the grateful offering of Melistion.
Anonymous epigrammatists
Do not speak, and you will speak my name. But must you speak it?
Then thus again—a great marvel—speaking, you will speak my name.
Simias

To be written thus: A gift to man-goddess Athena the Phocian gave, repaying the grace of mighty counsel, at that time when, with fire-breathing wax, he set ablaze the holy city — not counted among the foremost fighters of the Achaeans, but now he has gone upon the Homeric road, thrice blessed, on whom in your heart this happiness breathes ever. Look graciously about us. For your grace, holy and full-counselling Pallas; but, in disgrace, bring the stream from the pure springs; of the sons of Dardanus, and the gold-dyed lords he hurled from their foundations; Epeius gave the axe, with which once he cast down the height of the god-built towers.
To be read thus:

A gift to man-goddess Athena the Phocian gave, repaying the grace of mighty counsel, Epeius gave the axe, with which once he cast down the height of the god-built towers, at that time when, with fire-breathing wax, he set ablaze the holy city of the sons of Dardanus, and the gold-dyed lords he hurled from their foundations; — not counted among the foremost fighters of the Achaeans, but, in disgrace, brought the stream from the pure springs upon the road; but now he has gone upon the Homeric road, for your grace, holy and full-counselling Pallas; thrice blessed, on whom in your heart you look graciously about us. This happiness breathes ever.
Anonymous Epigrammatists
A pillar of good order and an offering of temperance, the image of Nicholas Gregory set up.
Asclepiades
Upon the tetrameter formed from a regular trimeter by the addition of a final foot, a curtailed trimeter O passer-by, even if you are in some haste, stop a moment, I beg you, and hear
how great, indeed, was the sorrow of Botrys,
who, an old man of eighty years, buried his son of nine,
a child already wise and skilled in speech.
Alas for the father, and alas for you too, dear child of Botrys,
bereft of how many pleasures you have perished.
Anonymous epigrammatists
Child of Nereus though I am, the son of Earth bears me up,
as I sink down into the lovely streams of Styx.
Anonymous Epigrammatists

On the book of Mark If you wish to master grief, unfolding this blessed book go through it carefully, beneath whose most blessed judgement readily you will see the things to come, the things that are and the things gone by, that delight and pain alike are nothing better than smoke.
Simonides
a. Tell me, who are you, whose son, of what homeland, and what do you win? b. Casmylus, son of Evagoras, in the Pythian boxing, a Rhodian.
Callimachus
An eleven-syllable line upon the last metron of the foregoing tetrameter The gifts to Aphrodite.
Simon, the wanderer, dedicated her own image,
and the girdle
that loved her breasts, and the torch,
and the thyrsi she once tossed aloft,
shrieking, poor woman, up among the hills.
Anonymous epigrammatists
. . . you see me, Dionysus; a twofold womb
bore me, and my father is the lord of memory.
First it bore me a beast-bearer, pitiless of heart;
but when I had slain the dear son of a roe, my own sister's,
no longer do I bear the beast, but heaven and sea,
and earth, and the holy chorus of the blessed, deathless forever.
Simias

Behold me, lord of deep-bosomed Earth, who set the son of Acmon elsewhere, and do not tremble, though so great, that I am laden with shaggy thick beard. For I came to be at the time when Necessity ruled, and all things yielded to Earth's grievous designs, the creeping things, all that creep through the air. And of Chaos I am born; not the child of Cypris, swift-flying, nor am I called of Ares; for I ruled not by force, but by soft-spoken persuasion; and Earth yielded to me, and the recesses of the Sea, and the brazen Heaven; from these I took for myself the primeval sceptre, and I ordained the laws for the gods.
Simonides
This is the fair statue of fair Milon, who at Pisa seven times won, and never fell upon his knees.
Callimachus
Upon the doubled metron, an epodic tetrameter, exceeding the hexameter by one syllable To Demeter of the Gates, for whom Acrisius
once built this temple, not the Pelasgian one, these gifts
did Timodemus of Naucratis set up,

a wide-wandering creeper from the head of the well-fleeced beast.
Arabius
On the image of Helen The lovely likeness of Argive Helen, whom once a herdsman carried off, thrusting aside Zeus the god of strangers.
Anonymous epigrammatists
An oracle given to Aegeus, who asked concerning the begetting of children The jutting foot of the wineskin, dearest of men,
do not loose, until you come to the height of Athens.
Pollianus

This is the Polyxena of Polycleitus, nor did any other hand touch this divine panel. It is the sister-work of Hera. See how, with her robe rent, she hides her bared modesty with a chaste veil; the wretched one pleads for her life; and in the eyes of the maiden lies the whole war of the Phrygians.
Anonymous Epigrammatists

On the image of Dido You behold the original of glorious Dido, stranger, an image shining with divine beauty. Such indeed I was; but I had not the mind, such as you hear, having won my fame on honourable grounds. For I never set eyes on Aeneas, nor in the time of Troy's sacking did I come to Libya; but, fleeing the violence of Iarbas' marriage, I drove the two-edged sword into my heart. Pierians, why did you arm holy Maro against me, who lied so against my chastity?
Gauradas

Dear Echo, agree with me in something. — In what? I love a girl; but she does not love me. — She loves you. And the moment does not bring the chance to act. — It brings it. Then you, tell her that I love her. — I love her. And give her some pledge of money. — Give it. Echo, what remains, but to win my desire? — To win it.
Satyrus
On the statue of Echo Through the shepherd's meadow tongueless Echo sings, answering the birds with her late-following voice.
Archias

On the same You see rocky Echo, friend, companion of Pan, the answering voice that sings back in reverse, the chattering image of all manner of mouths, a sweet plaything for shepherds. Whatever you say, hearing this, go away.
Euodus
On the same Echo, the mimic of speech, the dregs of the voice, the tail of a word.
Anonymous Epigrammatists
Julianus
On the armed Athena in Athens Why, Tritogeneia, are you helmeted in the midst of the city? Poseidon has yielded; spare the land of Cecrops.
Diotimus

As is fitting, I am Artemis; and the bronze itself well declares Artemis the daughter of Zeus, and of no other. Reckon the boldness of the maiden. Truly you might say: "All the earth is too small a hunting-ground for her."
Anonymous Epigrammatists

On the statue of Aphrodite in Cnidus Who gave soul to the stone? Who saw Cypris upon the earth? Who wrought such desire in the rock? This is the work of Praxiteles' hands, surely, or perhaps Olympus is widowed, since the Paphian has come to Cnidus.
Plato

On the same The Paphian Cytherea came through the waves to Cnidus, wishing to behold her own image; and gazing all about in the conspicuous place, she cried: "Where did Praxiteles see me naked?" Praxiteles saw not what was unlawful; but the iron carved her as Ares would have wished the Paphian.
Plato
Neither Praxiteles fashioned you, nor the iron; but you stood thus, just as once when you were judged.
Anonymous Epigrammatists
Cypris, when she saw Cypris in Cnidus, said: "Alas, alas! Where did Praxiteles see me naked?"
Pseudo-Lucianus
No one has seen the Paphian naked; but if anyone has seen her, it is this man who set up the naked Paphian.
Pseudo-Lucianus
To you I dedicated the most beautiful image of your form, Cypris, having nothing finer than your form.
Euenus
Pallas and the consort of the son of Cronus said, when they saw the Cnidian: "We blame the Phrygian unjustly."
Euenus

Before, on the Idaean hills, the herdsman himself beheld her who first bore off the prize of beauty; but Praxiteles set her, all-visible, before the Cnidians, holding the vote of Paris as witness of his art.
Antipater

You will say, beholding Cypris on rugged Cnidus, that, stone though she is, she will set even stone afire; but seeing the sweet Eros of desire among the Thespians, that he will cast fire even into cold adamant. Such gods Praxiteles wrought, one in one land and one in another, that all might not be scorched with double fire.
Anonymous Epigrammatists
Anonymous Epigrammatists

On the same, and on the Athena in Athens Look round on the sacred beauty of the foam-born Paphian, and you will say: "I praise the Phrygian for his judgement." Looking again at the Attic Pallas, you will cry this: "How did the herdsman Paris pass her by?"
Hermodorus

On the same Seeing the Cnidian Cytherea, stranger, you would say this: "She herself rules both mortals and immortals." But seeing in the city of Cecrops the spear-bold Pallas, you will declare: "Truly Paris was a herdsman."
Leonidas

On Aphrodite armed These arms of Ares, for what reason, O Cytherea, have you put on, bearing this empty weight? For naked you disarmed Ares himself; and if even a god is undone, in vain you bring arms against men.
Alexander
Pallas herself, surely, perfected Cypris, forgetting the judgement upon Alexander.
Julianus

On the armed Aphrodite in Sparta Always Cytherea has learned to bear the quiver, the bow, and the work of the long-range shaft; but, respecting the laws of war-steadfast Lycurgus, she brings to Sparta her love-charms in close-fighting arms. And you in your chambers, Spartan women, revering the arms of Cythera, bring forth bold children.
Anonymous Epigrammatists
On the same Pallas, when she saw Cytherea armed, said: "Cypris, will you have us thus go to the judgement?" And she, laughing gently: "Why should I lift a shield against you?"
Anonymous Epigrammatists
Either the Paphian, stone as she is, armed herself, or rather, perhaps, the Paphian saw the stone, and swore she wished to be it.
Antipater

Cypris too is in Sparta; not as in other cities is she set up, clothed in soft folds; but on her head she has a helmet instead of a veil, and instead of golden boughs a spear-shaft. For the consort of Thracian Enyalius and a Lacedaemonian should not be without arms.
Philippus

Smile-loving Cypris, tender of the bridal chamber, who crowned you, the honeyed deity, with the arms of war? Dear to you was the paean, and golden-haired Hymenaeus, and the sweet-singing graces of the clear pipes. Why have you put on these man-killing arms? Do you boast, having despoiled bold Ares, how much Cypris can do?
Antipater

On the same, rising from the sea The Cypris but now rising from her mother the sea, behold the labour of Apelles' pencil, how, gathering her sea-soaked hair with her hand, she wrings the foam from her wet locks.
Archias
On the same Apelles saw Cypris herself, naked, being born from the sea, her nurse, and fashioned her thus, drenched with the water's foam, still wringing her locks with her blooming hands.
Democritus

On the same When Cypris, her hair dripping with the brine-flowing foam, naked rose from the purple wave, thus, surely, taking her tresses in her hands by her white cheeks, she squeezed out the Aegean sea, showing her breast alone, which is lawful; but if such is she, let the spirit of Enyalius be confounded.
Julianus

On the same But now the Paphian rose forth from her sea-birth, finding the hand of Apelles for her midwife. But withdraw quickly from the pencils, lest the foam dripping from her wrung locks wet you. If such a Cypris once was made naked for the apple, unjustly did Pallas ravage Troy.
Leonidas

On the same Her who had escaped from her mother's bosom, still murmuring with foam, well-bedded Cypris, Apelles, seeing the most lovely beauty, fashioned her not painted but alive. For well with her fingertips she wrings her hair, and well from her eyes a calm desire shines forth, and her breast, the herald of her prime, is firm as the quince; and Athena herself and the consort of Zeus will say: "O Zeus, we are surpassed in the judgement."
Anonymous Epigrammatists
On a statue of Dionysus standing near Athena

a. Tell me, what have you in common with Pallas? For to her belong javelins and wars, but to you feasts are pleasing. b. Not rashly, stranger, ask such things about the gods; know in how many ways I am like this deity. For mine too is the dear glory of wars; the Indian knows me, subdued from the eastern Ocean, and we both ennoble the life of men, she with the olive, but I with the sweet clusters of the cultivated vine. And indeed not even for me did my mother endure birth-pangs: I loosed my father's thigh, she his head.
Antipater

On another statue of the same As fellow-shieldsman to Italian Piso, Dionysus I am set up, the guardian of the halls, for good fortune. "Worthily, O Dionysus, you entered the house." Both befitted: the hall for Bacchus, and Bromius for the hall.
Anonymous Epigrammatists

On the statue of Dionysus and Heracles Both from Thebes, and both warriors, and from Zeus; the one terrible with the thyrsus, the other with the club. Their pillars stand together; their arms are alike, the fawnskin to the lion-skin, the cymbals to the clapper. Hera was a harsh goddess to both. And both, from the earth, came to the immortals out of the fire.
Xenocritus

On the statue of Hermes Swift Hermes am I called; but in the wrestling-school do not set me up maimed of hands, nor footless; or how am I swift? How shall I gesture upright with my hands, standing orphaned of both for a base?
Anonymous Epigrammatists
On the same A man prayed to a wooden Hermes, and it was wood. Then, lifting it, he dashed it to the ground; and from it gold streamed when it broke. Insolence has often brought gain.
Nicias

Having my lot in the leaf-shaking, steep mountain of Cyllene, here I stand, the guardian of the lovely gymnasium, Hermes; over whom the boys often laid marjoram and hyacinth, and fresh garlands of violets.
Anonymous Epigrammatists

A guardian over the beehives, for the sake of Peristratus, I remain here, having left the Maenalian slope, watching for the thief of the bees. But beware my hand, and the light reach of my countryman's foot.
Leonidas
Morichus the goatherd set up Hermes the overseer as the well-reputed guardian of his flocks. But, O you that have fed upon the green woodland on the hills, have no care for the ravenous wolf.
Nicaenetus
A turning circle of the potter's wheel moulded me here, an earthen Hermes, with earthen feet. I was kneaded of clay; I will not lie. But I loved, stranger, the ill-fated work of the potters.
Anonymous Epigrammatists
O best of men, do not think you behold one of the many images of Hermes; for I am the work of Scopas.
Philippus

a. May I touch the cabbage, Cyllenian? b. No, passer-by. a. What grudge over vegetables? b. No grudge, but a law, to keep thieving hands off others' property. a. O strange thing: Hermes has made a new law, not to steal!
Palladas
On the statue of Eros Someone brought a bronze Eros out of fire into fire, fitting a frying-pan as a torture for the torturer.
Satyrus

On a statue of the same, bound Who fettered the winged one here, who bound in chains the swift fire? Who laid hold of the flaming quiver, and shackled the swift-shooting, all-encircling hands, binding them to a sturdy column? These are cold comforts for men. May not this prisoner himself once have bound that one's heart?
Alcaeus

On the same Who fettered you here, unholily caught, and set you up? Who bound your hands in a tangle, and made your face squalid? Where are your swift arrows, foolish one? Where the bitter, fire-bearing quiver? In vain, surely, the stone-carver toiled, who bound you, who once stirred the gods with desire, in this snare.
Antipater

On the same Who bound your hands to the column with inescapable knots? Who took fire with fire, and guile with guile? Foolish one, do not let a tear fall down your sweet face; for you delight in the tears of young men.
Quintus Maecius

On the same Weep, your hands bound past escape, reckless deity, weep much, dripping soul-melting tears, you insulter of temperance, mind-stealer, robber of reason, winged fire, unseen wound of the soul, Eros. For mortals your bond is a release from their groans, reckless one; bound by it, send your prayers to the deaf winds. And the unguarded fire you kindled in mortals' hearts, behold now quenched by your own tears.
Crinagoras

On the same Both weep and groan, your sinews bound together by your hands, you schemer; such things befit you. There is none to loose you; do not look up smoothly. For you yourself wrung from the eyes of others the tear, and fixing bitter shafts in the heart, you dripped the venom of inescapable longings, Eros; and the woes of mortals are laughter to you. You have suffered such things as you did. Justice is good.
Moschus

On Eros ploughing Laying aside torch and bow, shaggy Eros took up the ox-driving goad, and had a wallet on his shoulder, and, yoking the patient necks of bulls beneath the yoke, he sowed the wheat-bearing furrow of Deo. And looking up he said to Zeus himself: "Fill the fields, lest I cast you, the bull of Europa, beneath the plough."
Marianus

On Eros crowned Where is that back-bent bow of yours, and the reeds that, shot from you, fix themselves in the very heart? Where are your wings? Where the much-paining torch? And why three garlands do you hold in your hands, and bear another on your head? — "Not from the common Cypris, stranger, nor from the earth am I, nor the offspring of woodland mirth; but I kindle in the pure mind of men the torch of good learning, and lead the soul up to heaven. And from the virtues I weave four crowns; from each of which bearing these, I am crowned first with that of wisdom."
Anonymous Epigrammatists

On the same Do not call me, stranger, the one from Lebanon, the revel-lover who delights in the night-time talk of young men; I am a humble countryman from a neighbouring Nymph, urging on only the works of planting. Whence from the fruitful, dear vineyard four garlands of the Seasons crowned me, four in number.
Julianus

On the Eros of Praxiteles Bending his proud neck beneath our sandals, Praxiteles fashioned me with plundering hands. For Eros himself, who lies hidden within me, he forged in bronze, and gave to Phryne as a gift of love; and she again brought him to Eros; for it is lawful for lovers to bring Eros himself as a gift to Eros.
Simonides

On the same Praxiteles made exact the Eros that he suffered, drawing the original from his own heart, giving me to Phryne as the price of myself. And I breed love-charms no longer by shooting, but by being gazed upon.
Tullius Geminus

On the same In return for love, Praxiteles gave Eros, a god, to mortal Phryne, finding both his fee and a god. And she did not refuse the maker; for her heart feared lest the god take up allied arms in place of art. But she no longer dreads the Eros of Cypris, but the one from you, Praxiteles, knowing art to be his mother.
Leonidas

On the same The Thespians revere Eros as the only god from Cytherea, painted from no other original, but the one Praxiteles knew as a god; whom, gazing about Phryne, he gave as the ransom of his own longings.
Palladas
Gabrielius
On Eros sleeping in a bed of pepper Not even in slumber, nor breathless, nor at a feast is Eros free from his fire-sown sting.
Anonymous Epigrammatists
You who blow upon the brand to light your lamp, come, light it from my soul; for I am all aflame.
Plato

When we came to the deep-shaded grove, we found within the child of Cythera, like to purple apples. He had no quiver holding arrows, no curved bow; but these hung upon the well-leaved trees, and he himself, fettered in sleep among the rose-cups, slept smiling; and overhead the tawny bees sprinkled upon his sweet lips their wax-poured honey.
Statyllius Flaccus

On Eros sleeping You sleep, bringing sleepless cares upon mortals; you sleep, ah child of the baneful Foam-born, not lifting the fiery pine-torch, nor unguarded plucking the shaft from your counter-stretched bow. Let others take heart; but I, proud one, am afraid, lest even in your slumber you see some bitter dream of me.
Alpheus

On the same I shall snatch the fiery torch, Eros, from your hand, I shall strip the quiver that hangs about your shoulders, if truly you sleep, offspring of fire, and your men I lead to a little good order of the bow. But even so I fear you, schemer, lest you hide some plot against me, and even in sleep see a bitter dream.
Straton

Even if swift wings are stretched about your back, and Scythian arrow-points dart from your bow, I shall flee you, Eros, beneath the earth. But what good? For not even all-subduing Hades himself escaped your might.
Secundus

On statues of Loves See the spoil-loving Loves, see how upon their sturdy shoulders they bear the arms of the gods, the babes exulting: the drums and the thyrsus of Bromius, and the thunderbolt of Zeus, the shield of Enyalius and his fair-crested helmet, the well-bowed quiver of Phoebus, the trident of the Sea, and the club of the strong hands of Heracles. What more for men, when Eros has even taken the sky, and Cypris has plundered the arms of the immortals?
Philippus

Having despoiled Olympus, see how the Loves adorn themselves with the arms of the immortals, exulting in their spoils. They bear the bow of Phoebus, and the thunderbolt of Zeus, the weapon and helmet of Ares, the club of Heracles, and the club of the god, the three-barbed spear, and the thyrsus of Bacchus, the winged sandals of Hermes, the torches of Artemis. It is no burden for mortals to yield to the shafts of the Loves, to whom the gods have given the ornament of arms to hold.
Parmenion

On the statue of Hera Argive Polycleitus, who alone beheld Hera with his eyes and, having seen all that he saw, fashioned her, showed her beauty to mortals, as far as is lawful; but the forms hidden beneath her robe, unknown, are kept for Zeus.
Anonymous Epigrammatists
On the statue of Calliope I am Calliope; and to Cyrus I gave my breast, who reared divine Homer, whence sweet Orpheus drank.
Joannes Barbucallus
The painter wished to draw Melpomene in the image, but, falling short, he painted Calliope.
Joannes Barbucallus
This image is yours, Polymnia, and yet it is also the Muse's; for over both there is one name and one likeness.
Antipater

On images of the Muses We three Muses stand here; one bears the pipes, one in her hands the lyre, and one the tortoise-shell. The one holds the lyre of Aristocles, the one of Ageladas the barytone, and the one of Canachas the hymn-singing reeds. But the one is mistress of the tone, the other the singer of the melody, and the other the inventor of wise harmony.
Theaetetus

On the Nemesis of the Athenians Me, a snow-white stone, from the ever-growing crag the Mede, having cut me with stone-cutting points, carried over the sea, that he might make of me a man's likeness, the token of his triumph over the Athenians. But when Marathon clashed back at the slaughtered Persians, and the ships sailed the watery ways on bloody streams, the noblest Athens carved me into Adrasteia, a deity opposed to overweening men. I weigh hopes against hope; and I am even now victory for the sons of Erechtheus, Nemesis for the Assyrians.
Parmenion

On the same Hoped by the Medes to be a trophy-bearing stone, I was changed in form, fittingly, into Nemesis, set up, a just goddess, on the banks of Rhamnus, a witness for Attica of victory and of wisdom.
Anonymous Epigrammatists
On the statue of Nemesis Nemesis forewarns, by her cubit-rule and by her bridle, to do nothing beyond measure, nor to speak things unbridled.
Anonymous Epigrammatists
On the same I, Nemesis, hold a cubit-rule; for what reason, you will ask. I proclaim to all: nothing beyond the measure.
Arabius

On the statue of Pan One might almost have heard distinctly Pan piping, for the sculptor mingled breath into the figure; but, seeing wandering Echo flee, helpless, ever-shifting, he refused the useless note of the pipe.
Alcaeus

On the same Breathe, Pan, with your sweet lips the mountain-ranging Muse, breathe, delighting in the shepherd's reed, pouring melody from the tuneful pipe, and from the accompanying strain ring out, guiding the harmony of the word; and around you, to the rhythm's beat, let the inspired step be danced for these water-dwelling Nymphs.
Anonymous Epigrammatists

Here, cast down upon the green meadow, traveller, rest your soft limbs from your weary toil, where the pine, shaken by the breezes of Zephyrus, will charm you, as you listen to the cicadas' song; and the shepherd in the mountains, piping near the spring at midday, beneath the shade of a leafy plane-tree; and, fleeing the heat of the autumn Dog-star, you will cross the height in season. Heed Hermes, who tells you this.
Anyte
Anonymous Epigrammatists
Leonidas

Do not, traveller, drink here this warm water of the gully, full of mud from the sheep-pasture; but go a little beyond this heifer-grazed height, there, beside that shepherd's pine, and you will find, gurgling through the fair-fountained rock, a stream colder than the northern snow.
Anyte
a. Why, Pan the hunter, sitting in the lonely, shady wood, do you play upon this sweet-voiced reed? b. That over these dewy mountains my heifers may graze, plucking the fair-haired ears of corn.
Simonides
Me, the goat-footed Pan, the Arcadian, who am against the Medes, who am with the Athenians, Miltiades set up.
Theaetetus

On the same Wood-walker, lover of trees, husband of mountain-dwelling Echo, Pan, the watchman, the guardian of the well-horned flock, Pan the rough-shanked, the much-sowing, who, as a migrant, ran to the battle of the Assyrian spearmen, when Miltiades set me up, the Persian-driving comrade in arms, I stand, the guest-gift of an uncalled alliance. To others the citadels; but the Mede-slaying Marathon is shared by me and by the Marathon-fighters.
Philodemus

The stone holds three immortals; for the head clearly reveals Pan the goat-horned, the breast and belly Heracles, and the rest of the thighs and the shin fell to the lot of winged-footed Hermes. You will refuse, stranger, to sacrifice no more; for from your one victim we three deities have our portion.
Apollonides

I am a god of the countryside; why do you pour libations to me in golden cups, and pour the Italian wine of Bromius, and bind to the rock the round necks of bulls? Spare them; I do not delight in such sacrifices. I am Pan of the hillside, of plain wood, a feaster on lambs, and a drinker of the earthen cup of new wine.
Peritas
Here upon the dry-stone walls Deinomenes set up the wakeful Priapus, the guardian of his vegetables. But, thief, see how I am erect. "This," you ask, "for the sake of a few vegetables?" Of the few.
Tymnes

On the statue of Priapus I do my Priapic part to everything, even if it is Cronus; I make no distinction of any thief in any way here beside these garden-beds. "It is unseemly to say these things for the sake of vegetables and gourds," someone will say. It was unseemly; but I say it.
Pseudo-Lucianus
For form's sake Eutychides set me here, this Priapus, the guardian of dry vine-twigs; and I have a deep precipice round about me. Whoever comes, has nothing to steal but me, the guardian.
Apollonides
Anaxagoras set me up, the Priapus not upon his feet, but kneeling on both knees on the ground; Philomachus made me. But seeing fair Charito near me, seek no longer how I fell.
Philippus

a. The figs look ripe; if you would let me take a few. b. Touch not a single one. a. How angry Priapus is! b. You will say more, and go away empty. a. Yes, I beseech you. b. Give me; for I too am in want. a. Do you need anything from me, tell me? b. There is some law: give and take. a. And you, a god, in need of money? b. I love another thing. a. What is this? b. Eating my own figs, give me cheerfully the dried fig in return.
Marcus Argentarius
Erycius

On the same How heavy, Priapus, and well-knotted, is this weapon, which you have poured forth, all of it, from your groin, ready for marriage; and a thirst for women holds you, my good fellow, and your whole soul swells with longings. But calm this swollen member, and hide it beneath a flowery cloak; for you dwell on no lonely mountain, but beside Helle's holy shore you tend Lampsacus.
Antistius

A field-guard I stand in rich-yielding fields, saving Phricon's hut and his plants, saying this to each one: "When you have laughed, seeing me and my equipment, go your own way. But if you trespass to what is unlawful, the hairy thing will be no help to you; we know how to pierce all men."
Agathias Scholasticus

On the image of a Satyr holding a pipe to his ear and as if listening By itself, little Satyr, does your reed send forth sound? Or why do you bend your ear and lead it to the pipe? And he, laughing, kept silent; perhaps he would have spoken, but he was held by the forgetfulness of his delight. For no wax stopped him; willingly he embraced silence, turning his whole heart to the business of the pipe.
Leontius Minotaurus
Dionysus, seeing the Satyr in such pain, and pitying him, made him of stone. But not even so did he cease from his heavy-burdened pains; for still he toils, even being stone, the wretched one.
Anonymous Epigrammatists
Either the Satyr crept beneath the bronze, or by art the bronze, compelled, was poured around the Satyr.
Neilus
On the image of a Satyr made of mosaic in Antioch

a. All Satyrs are mockers; but tell me, you too, why, looking at each one, do you pour out this laughter? b. Held by wonder I laugh, how, gathered from stone, piece by piece from here and there, I suddenly became a Satyr.
Plato
Diodorus put the Satyr to sleep, he did not carve him. If you prod him, you will wake him; the silver holds sleep.
Anonymous Epigrammatists
Beholding this fair image, Aphrodite, man, propitiate her, sitting near; and praise Glycera, daughter of Dionysius, who dedicated me beside the soft wave of the purple shore.
Anonymous Epigrammatists
On Eros See how the winged one breaks the winged thunderbolt, showing that fire is stronger than fire, Eros.
Anonymous Epigrammatists

Who fashioned a winged Eros facing the winged Eros? Nemesis, warding off bow with bow, that he might suffer what he did; and the bold one, once fearless, weeps, having tasted the bitter shafts, and thrice spat into his deep bosom. Ah, a great marvel: one shall kindle fire with fire; Eros has touched Eros.
Anonymous Epigrammatists
I too am of Cypris' blood; my mother bade me bear bow and wings against my brother.
Anonymous Epigrammatists
On Artemis

a. Artemis, where is your bow, and the quiver at your neck? And where the buskin of your Lycastian shoes, and the brooch wrought of gold, and the purple robe that winds down to the back of your knee? b. Those I arm myself with for the hunt; but to the sacrifices I go just as I am, meeting the holy offerings.
Anonymous Epigrammatists

On Hermes A holy heap of stone the passers-by poured up for me, Hermes; and in return for the little I felt for them no great gratitude, but only that the rest of the way to the fountain of Aex I reckon seven stades.
Anonymous Epigrammatists

Traveller, do not creep up to the vine-twigs, nor to the apples, nor where the medlars are; but there, toward the rushes, pass by, that you may break nothing of these, nor pluck off what with toil the planter Midon has won, who set me here too; and if you do not heed me, you will know Hermes, how I requite the wicked.
Anonymous Epigrammatists

I hold a rugged and lonely spot, traveller; not I, but Archelochus who set me here is to blame. For you did not rush as a mountain-lover, nor a hilltop-dweller, but rather, sir, content with the footpaths. And Archelochus, being himself a lover of solitude and neighbourless, O passer-by, set me too to dwell beside him so.
Anonymous Epigrammatists
On Dionysus From the fire, O Dionysus, behold, a second time in bronze you have appeared; Myron has found another birth for you.
Anonymous Epigrammatists

On Pan At the fire-offering of Dictynna's shrine the Cretan set me up in bronze, Pan the goat-hooved. I have a skin, and a double hare-club; and from a rocky cave I stretch a double gaze toward the mountain.
Anonymous Epigrammatists
From Parian stone the Athenians set me up on the height of Pallas' city, Pan the trophy-bearer.
Anonymous Epigrammatists

If I, Priapus, see you set your feet near the vegetables, I will strip you bare, thief, on the very garden-bed. "It is shameful to do this work," you will say; I know it myself, a god; but I was set up, you should know, for this shameful purpose.
Leonidas
By both roads I stand, Priapus, a guardian, my club raised straight up from my thighs. For Theocritus set me up to be faithful; but far off go, thief, lest you weep when you take my vein.

The goat-footed one, who lifts the wine-skin, and the laughing Nymphs, of Praxiteles, and the fair Danaë. All of white marble, and the work of supremely skilful hands. Momus himself will declare: "Father Zeus, this wisdom is unmixed."
